title: Relembre a palestra: Governança de Dados Mestres em ambientes SAP #SITCWB2026
author: AdrianoCWB
text:
No dia 7 de novembro, no Auditório Gregor Mendel da PUCPR, Paulo Cordeiro, fundador e SEO da 4MDG, especialista em governança de dados e MDM, apresentou no SAP Inside Track Curitiba 2026 a palestra "Governança de Dados Mestres em ambientes SAP: como melhorar a qualidade dos cadastros e reduzir custos". 
 Sobre a palestra 
 A tese da palestra está no título: a IA não inventa do nada, ela repete com confiança o que encontra na base da empresa. Paulo abriu com o caso Moffatt contra a Air Canada: o chatbot da companhia informou uma política de desconto errada, e em fevereiro de 2024 um tribunal da Colúmbia Britânica decidiu que quem responde pelo que a IA diz é a empresa (cerca de CA$ 812). Se a IA responde com base nos seus dados, quem responde pelos dados é você. 
 Ele citou também números do mercado: segundo o Gartner, 60% dos projetos de IA sem dados prontos para IA seriam abandonados até 2026, e a perda média anual por dados de baixa qualidade é de US$ 12,9 milhões. 
 Como a IA lê a sua empresa 
 Vetor e embedding: o texto vira coordenadas, e textos parecidos ficam perto. 
 Cadastro duplicado: três cadastros do mesmo fornecedor ficam colados no mapa, e a IA pode escolher o errado. Perto no significado não quer dizer certo no fato. 
 RAG: a IA responde com os seus documentos. O modelo é o mesmo para todos, a base é só sua. 
 Seis tendências de MDM 
 Stewardship autônomo com IA generativa: o steward define as políticas. 
 Resolução de entidades em tempo real. 
 MDM federado e composable. 
 Interfaces em linguagem natural, como Joule e CLAIRE. 
 Knowledge graphs e GraphRAG cross-domain. 
 MDM como fundação da governança de IA. 
 E a SAP nisso tudo 
 Paulo mostrou a SAP em três camadas (aplicações, dados e IA), a compra da Reltio (anunciada em 27/03/2026 e concluída em 07/05/2026) e o Gartner Magic Quadrant de MDM de abril de 2026, em que o SAP MDG aparece como Desafiante. A pergunta que ele deixou para quem opera SAP: como a SAP vai integrar MDG e Reltio, e qual será o roadmap de convergência? 
 Para levar 
 O steward muda de papel: define políticas, valida exceções e supervisiona modelos. 
 Qualidade de dados vira operação contínua, de remediar para prevenir. 
 Sem dados mestres limpos e governados, a IA amplifica erros em escala. 
 A IA pode executar e sugerir, mas assumir a responsabilidade pelo dado é uma decisão humana. 
 Sobre o palestrante 
 Paulo Cordeiro, fundador e SEO da 4MDG, autor do livro Master Data Management: Fundamentos e Aplicações e fundador da MDM Academy. Site: paulocordeiromdm.com.br.

title: How the Atlas Copco Group Makes Skills Visible Throughout the Organization
author: Patricia Bueters
text:
Skills have long played a role in talent-related decisions. For the Atlas Copco Group, the challenge lay in making them more visible and usable across the entire organization. 
 Turn HR into a strategic growth engine with AI 

 Learn how 

 With 56,000 employees in more than 70 countries, the decentralized industrial technology group is working with SAP SuccessFactors and TechWolf to establish a common framework for skills. This gives employees a better overview of opportunities within the Group, while providing the organization with greater insight into the skills available. 

 Skills were already part of the HR approach 

 Atlas Copco Group develops products, services, and solutions across four business areas. Its technologies range from compressed air and vacuum solutions to industrial power tools and machine vision. In 2025, the Group achieved a turnover of 168 billion SEK. 

 “We were already a skills-enabled organization,” said Emma Mercer, Group Talent & Learning Professional at the Atlas Copco Group. “Skills already play a role in decisions regarding recruitment, performance reviews, learning, career development, and succession planning.” 

 The aim was to make skills more visible within the Group and to link that information to the job architecture and HR processes. One of the triggers was the European directive on pay transparency. When Atlas Copco Group reviewed its job architecture with a view toward greater transparency, skills emerged as one of the factors relevant to determining the value of work. As a result, the discussion about skills took on a concrete business and compliance perspective. 

 Skills complement roles at Atlas Copco Group 

 The Atlas Copco Group deliberately describes its approach as “skills-enabled” rather than “skills-based.” Jobs and roles continue to provide structure to the organization. 

 “Jobs remain the foundation of the way we organize work today,” Mercer explained. “Skills add an extra layer to this, creating greater visibility.” 

 That extra layer can reveal competencies that aren’t apparent from a job title. Naomi Persoone, HR Digitalization Lead at Atlas Copco Group, uses her own role as an example: “My job title is HR Digital Lead, but I think people still have no idea what that actually entails. If we can translate that role into skills, we’re speaking a language that’s much easier to understand.” 

 The same principle applies to recruitment. Recruiters have always looked at what candidates can do. Data on skills makes those competencies more explicit and provides recruiters with additional information when assessing candidates. 

 SAP SuccessFactors and TechWolf lay the foundations for a shared approach to skills 

 SAP SuccessFactors has formed the basis of the Atlas Copco Group’s global HR ecosystem since 2013. The Group wanted to integrate skills into the systems that employees already use, without introducing a separate skills environment. 

 TechWolf uses AI to derive skills from Atlas Copco Group data and labor market information. “A few years ago, a skills-enabled organization was, in practice, a nice idea, but nobody really knew how to go about it,” said Oliver Kay, Talent and Skills Technology Leader at TechWolf. “With AI and the platforms we have now, it’s becoming a reality.” 

 Employees do not need to build their skills profile from scratch. AI suggests an initial version, which they can review and adjust themselves. Mercer sees this as a key condition for adoption. “If we’d started with a blank sheet of paper and asked every employee, ‘What are your skills?’, we wouldn’t be here today.” 

 The profiles evolve as employees develop new competencies. For example, via the Skill Assistant in Microsoft Teams, someone who has worked extensively with Power BI might be suggested to add that skill to their profile. Once validated, the information is fed through to SAP SuccessFactors. 

 Applying skills in HR processes 

 The Atlas Copco Group began working with TechWolf in 2024. The teams did not wait for a complete skills framework to be finalized, but tested the approach using specific business cases while developing the necessary integrations. 

 Talent acquisition was one of the first areas of application. Job skill profiles clarify which competencies are required for a role. Skills identified in CVs provide recruiters with additional information when assessing applications. In an early pilot for roles within industrial technology, Atlas Copco Group saw an increase in the number of female applicants after skills were included more explicitly in job advertisements. 

 Skills also play a role in performance enablement. They offer employees and managers a more concrete basis for development discussions and help to translate general development ambitions into specific competencies that an individual wishes to develop further. 

 Internal mobility is also a priority. Employees can progress rapidly within Atlas Copco Group, but due to its decentralized structure, opportunities elsewhere within the Group are sometimes less visible. “It’s not just about what you’re looking for,” Mercer said. “It’s also about opportunities you didn’t realize you were looking for.” 

 Clearer picture of career opportunities for staff 

 Around 1,500 staff members are currently taking part in the employee experience pilot. Using SAP SuccessFactors growth portfolio, they can review their skills and indicate the areas in which they wish to develop further. Career exploration highlights potential next roles and allows staff to compare their current profile with the competencies required for a different role. 

 Staff from sales and marketing, among others, are taking part in the pilot. This was a deliberate choice: they are often on the move and are generally willing to provide open feedback. Within a few weeks, more than 70% were using the new features. 

 Atlas Copco Group intends to expand the application further, including to blue-collar staff. The Group does not expect every group of staff to engage with the technology in the same way. The communication and change management approach will therefore be tailored to different working environments. 

 Lessons from Atlas Copco Group’s skills approach 

 One of the lessons is that the business must be involved in keeping skills information up to date. “From an HR perspective, you’re sometimes a bit removed from the business, which means you can’t always specify exactly what we’re looking for,” explained Persoone. “You have to involve the business.” 

 Business leaders and subject matter experts therefore help to validate job skill profiles. When the nature of the work changes, the profiles must evolve accordingly. This continues to require input from the people closest to that work. 

 The Atlas Copco Group also opted for a collaborative approach during the roll-out. Employees, managers, and HR took part in the pilot schemes together, rather than rolling out a centrally devised approach through the organization via a traditional top-down approach. “The feedback was: ‘I’m so glad we’re exploring this together,’” Persoone said. “It’s not as if you’re simply telling us: from now on, this is how we’ll do it.” 

 From insight into skills to workforce intelligence 

 The Atlas Copco Group is now further expanding the use of skills within its HR processes. In the longer term, the Group aims to utilize workforce intelligence to better understand how skills requirements are evolving and to make more informed decisions regarding its workforce. 

 The relationship between people and technology will also play a role in this. Skills data can help the Atlas Copco Group determine where human expertise creates the most value and where technology can support the work. This development is still at an early stage. According to Mercer, the way the organization views talent will determine the next steps. 

 “Technology can make skills visible. It can highlight opportunities and support career progression,” she said. “But becoming a skills-enabled organization doesn’t start with the system. It starts with the way we think about talent.”

title: Less Code, More Context: How AI Is Reshaping the Developer Role
author: Maarten Rikken
text:
Software development is not the first profession to be reshaped by a new tool. 
 SAP TechEd in 2026: The Autonomous Enterprise Becomes a Reality 

 Read the innovation news guide 

 Spreadsheets enabled accountants to automate calculations, digital tools let film editors rearrange scenes without physically cutting and splicing film, and architectural software simplified the drawing of plans. 

 However, these tools did not remove the need to understand the goal, exercise professional judgment, and evaluate the result. 

 AI is introducing a comparable shift for developers: from carrying out every implementation step themselves toward defining requirements, shaping solutions, and validating outcomes. 

 As developers delegate more work to AI, where does their expertise matter most? We asked developers in the SAP community and speakers at SAP TechEd in 2026 how they see the shift. 

 Context matters 

 “Business context is more important than ever,” said Douglas Cezar Kuchler, SAP champion, SAP Solution Architecture, sovanta AG. 

 That means looking beyond the immediate task, according to Simon Coen, lead for SAP Cloud Technologies at j&s-soft AG: “You really need to understand the business processes involved and how the solution fits into the existing system landscape.” 

 Indeed, in interviews with 22 advanced AI users , GitHub found that developers see themselves less as “code producers” and more as “creative directors of code,” with the core skill shifting from implementation to orchestration and verification. Developers must think at the level of outcomes and systems, not snippets. 

 Dr. Eng. Tomasz Wilk, GDC Poland PBS SAP chief architect, said he already sees the change in his daily work: “I spend much less time on coding itself and much more time talking to customers, understanding their needs, defining requirements, testing, and validating results.” 

 There is also a change in what developers need to specify. “We are no longer primarily specifying classes, methods, or individual pieces of code. We are describing a use case, a step in a business process, or ultimately a business capability,” Wilk said. “We become less the implementer and more the person responsible for expressing the business intent clearly enough for AI to turn it into a working solution.” 

 AI can amplify an organization’s existing strengths and weaknesses . Without a clear understanding of users and their needs, accelerated code generation risks simply taking a team in the wrong direction faster. 

 Kuchler believes the business objective, not the requested output, should shape the solution. 

 Imagine a customer request for an order-monitoring report. AI could help deliver the report quickly. But understanding why the customer wants it might uncover a different opportunity: anticipating delivery risks and preventing customer dissatisfaction. For example, the developer could explore an architecture in which an AI agent accesses relevant SAP business data via a governed ABAP RAP service and uses predictive capabilities, such as SAP-RPT, to identify potential delivery risks. 

 “That requires understanding AI capabilities, enterprise agent architecture, business value and processes, data relationships, desired outcomes, and decision boundaries before designing the solution,” Kuchler said. “AI can help us build what we ask for. Understanding the business helps us discover what is actually worth building.” 

 The importance of business context isn’t new, but now AI needs it to be made explicit. Andrei Liakhavets, SAP developer at BeNeering, observed: “In the past, a lot of business context was not documented in any way, but directly translated from words into code.” With AI, he added, “that ‘documenting’ step is less avoidable.” 

 For Wilk, capturing business intent also matters when a solution needs to be migrated, regenerated, or redesigned. “If the original business intent and context were never captured precisely, we may reproduce the functionality but lose the reasoning behind it,” he said. “The new solution may look correct and still behave differently where it matters. The more implementation we delegate to AI, the more precisely we need to preserve the intent behind it.” 

 Design: turning context into a solution 

 Kuchler said AI is changing how developers divide their attention among business understanding, design, and implementation: “AI is changing the balance: we can increasingly guide implementation while concentrating on defining the right solution, its constraints and authorizations, and how to validate the results.” 

 Coen described the same shift: “The role of a developer is shifting more and more to defining problems, making architectural decisions, guiding, and evaluating rather than implementing.” 

 That means translating business understanding into both architectural decisions and implementation guidance. Sergio Guerrero, principal at Shockwave Consulting LLC, described combining business context and rules with technical instructions covering SAP Fiori best practices, CDS modeling, OData, and the application being built. That requires a view beyond individual generated components. 

 “Being able to understand a solution as a whole, rather than just small pieces of code, is fundamental while collaborating with AI tools,” Guerrero explained. “There was already a design step before AI. Now, designing has become more important.” 

 “At the same time, I do not think everything has to be perfectly defined upfront,” Wilk said. “AI can actually help us with the discovery itself.” Prototypes don’t need to offer any answer; they can “help the customer understand the problem better, challenge initial assumptions, and discover what they actually need.” 

 For Wilk, AI-first doesn’t mean approaching problems with “Where can we put an agent?” but rather with the problem in mind, then asking whether AI is the right solution. 

 Still building, still responsible 

 However, not every developer sees this as a shift from building to designing. Liakhavets sees it differently: “I do not like such wording. For me, designing is something theoretical, and building is the practical part. And with AI or without AI, it is still building. So, for me it is still building, just with a new tool.” 

 What hasn’t changed is responsibility. “You still need to understand what AI is doing, as you are responsible for its results,” Liakhavets said. 

 This responsibility extends through validation. “Developers need to connect business objectives with AI capabilities, design interactions between agents and enterprise systems, establish constraints and authorizations, and evaluate the quality and trustworthiness of outcomes,” Kuchler said. 

 For Coen, technical expertise remains essential: “You have to be able to challenge the outcome of the AI rather than simply accepting what was generated.” Business context helps define the right solution; engineering judgement helps establish whether AI has actually delivered it. 

 Work is changing, not value 

 AI is changing how developers build, but not what makes their work valuable. Understanding the business helps them identify the right problem, clear intent guides implementation, and technical judgment determines whether the result is fit for purpose. Context needs to guide the work through to validation. 

 The measure of success is not how much code AI can produce, but whether the resulting solution serves the business. 

 As Kuchler put it: “I’m becoming less focused on how much code I can produce, and much more interested in how much business value I can help create through software.”

title: Governing Data Products in SAP Business Data Cloud
author: hkaur
text:
Governing Data Products in SAP Business Data Cloud 
 Introduction 
 As organisations move toward treating data as a managed, shareable product, the question of who can access what data, under what conditions, and with what accountability becomes central. SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) addresses this through a structured governance model: one that balances self-service discovery for data consumers with controlled, auditable access managed by data stewards. 
 This blog provides a walkthrough of that governance model — the domain and terms framework, the access request lifecycle, and the row-level data controls applied within SAP Datasphere once a data product is installed. 
 The Governance Foundation: Domains and Ownership 
 The Governance option in the BDC cockpit is used by anyone acting in a data steward capacity. Through it, data stewards configure domains, define the terms and conditions governing data product usage, establish automatic approval workflows, and manage which users are granted access to which data products. 
 Domains allow organisations to define clear ownership of data products and set the terms and conditions for their usage. The default domain in BDC is the starting point for domain management. To access and edit domain configuration, a user requires global and scoped roles that grant the following privileges: BDC Data Packages (Read) to access the Domains page from the BDC cockpit; Cloud Data Product (Share) to access the Governance app. 
 Governance Personas 
 There are two primary personas in the BDC governance model, each with a clearly defined role in the access lifecycle: 

 Persona 
 Role in Governance 
 Key Actions 

 Catalog User 
 (Requester / Consumer) 
 Discovers and requests for access to data products 
 Accesses the Catalog & Marketplace from the BDC cockpit to find data products. Submits access requests specifying business reasons, target space, required endpoints, and optional expiration date. Installs approved data products to a Datasphere space. 

 Data Steward 
 (Catalog Administrator + BD Viewer roles) 
 Sets up and manages governance for data products 
 Manages domains and terms and conditions via the Governance app. Reviews and approves or rejects access requests in Governance → Access Management. Configures automatic approval settings. Monitors all active access agreements centrally. 
 Data Steward is a functional persona, not a named role in BDC. It is enabled by assigning a combination of global and scoped roles together, the recommended standard role combination is Catalog Administrator + BD Viewer. 
 Terms and Conditions: Standard and Custom 
 Before access requests can be submitted, the data steward must define the terms and conditions under which a data product may be used. Best practice is to set terms and conditions to ensure data is used appropriately and not exploited. BDC supports two types: 

 Type 
 Description 
 When to Use 

 Default (Standard) 
 Terms and Conditions 
 A standardised set of terms applied uniformly to all data products within a domain. 
 Low-risk, commonly used data. Ensure consistency at scale and reduces per-product overhead. Appropriate where a uniform usage policy covers all products in the domain. 

 Custom 
 Terms and Conditions 
 Product-specific terms that apply to a particular data product, overriding the domain default. 
 Sensitive, regulated, or commercially restricted data — such as products containing personal data subject to data protection regulations, or data with specific usage restrictions. 
 A consumer cannot submit an access request without reviewing and accepting the applicable terms, creating an auditable record of consent from the first step of the access lifecycle. 
 The Access Request Lifecycle 
 Once a data product is published to Catalog & Marketplace and terms are configured, access follows a formal four-stage lifecycle: 
 Access Request → Review / Approval → Access Agreement → Installation 
 Stage 1 — Access Request (Catalog User / Requester) 
 The consumer navigates to the Catalog & Marketplace in the BDC cockpit side navigation, selects the Data Products collection, and submits a request. The request must specify: 
 The reason for accessing that is business justification 
 The target tenant and Datasphere space where the data product will be installed 
 The specific endpoints (data entities) required 
 An optional expiration date for time-limited access 
 Stage 2 — Review / Approval (Data Steward) 
 The data steward navigates Governance Access Management in the BDC cockpit and selects the Requests tab, which is automatically filtered to show requests awaiting approval. The steward reviews the request details and either approves or rejects it. Data Stewards should follow their organisation’s data governance policies when reviewing requests and apply stricter controls for products containing sensitive or private data. 
 Manual vs. Automatic Approval 
 BDC supports configuring automatic approval for access requests. The option for automatic approval is best suited for standardised terms and low-risk data. Automatically approved requests still generate access agreements and are therefore still tracked for audit purposes. 
 Stage 3 — Access Agreement 
 An approved request — whether approved manually or automatically — converts to an access agreement. The access agreement is a persistent record that captures who requested access, which data product and endpoints were approved, the terms accepted, who approved it, and the validity period. Data stewards can view all active access agreements centrally in the BDC cockpit, providing complete visibility of data product consumption across the organisation. Access agreements are retained even after they expire or are ended. 
 Stage 4 — Installation 
 With an approved access agreement in place, the consumer can install the data product to the specified Datasphere space to make it available for modelling, analytics, and other use. 
 Rejected Requests and System-Created Requests 
 A rejected request cannot be edited — the consumer must submit a new request if access is still needed. Rejected requests are permanently deleted 90 days after the date they were created. If a request is not processed by its specified end date, it is automatically rejected. 
 Row-Level Security in SAP Datasphere: Data Access Controls 
 Installing a data product to a Datasphere space grants users access to the space and its objects — but it does not by itself control which rows of data each individual user may see within those objects. SAP Datasphere addresses this through Data Access Controls (DACs): a row-level security mechanism that filters the data returned to each user based on criteria defined in a permissions entity. 
 What Data Access Control Does 
 A data access control, once applied to a data layer view or business layer object, restricts the rows returned by that object to those matching the criteria defined in the permissions entity. The restriction applies consistently regardless of how the data is accessed: whether a user queries the protected object directly or reaches it through a downstream object that sources from it, only the records they are permitted to see are returned. The filtering is silent — no error or denial message is shown; the user's result set simply reflects their authorised scope. 
 Who Can Create Data Access Controls 
 Users with the DW Space Administrator role can create data access controls to allow modellers to apply row-level security to Data Builder and Business Builder objects within that space. 
 The Permissions Entity 
 The foundation of data access control is a permissions entity — a table or view in the Datasphere space that maps user identifiers to one or more filter criteria. The user identifier column contains the SAP Datasphere user IDs in the format required by the connected identity provider (such as email addresses, logon names, or other identifiers). Each row in the permissions entity defines which values a given user is authorised to see for the specified criteria column. 
 Permissions Entity Structures: Three Types 
 SAP Datasphere supports three structure types for data access control, each suited to different access patterns: 

 Structure 
 Behaviour 

 Single Values 
 Row visibility is limited to records whose value matches one of the discrete values assigned to that user in the permissions entity. 

 Hierarchy 
 Row visibility is scoped to the hierarchy nodes assigned to the user in the permissions entity, including all descendant nodes. Only external hierarchies defined with a single parent-child column pair are supported. 

 Hierarchy with Directory 
 Row visibility encompasses the user's assigned hierarchy nodes and all their descendants, resolved across one or more hierarchies through a directory structure. 
 Configuring Data Access Control: Steps 
 The setup of data access control in SAP Datasphere involves three sequential steps: 
 Step 1 — Prepare a permissions entity. Create a table or view that lists SAP Datasphere user IDs (in the format required by your identity provider) and assign them to one or more filter criteria columns. This entity must include an identifier column containing user IDs. 
 Step 2 — Create data access control. In the side navigation area, select Data Builder and choose New Data Access Control. Set the structure type (Single Values, Hierarchy, or Hierarchy with Directory), select the permissions entity, and designate the identifier column containing the user IDs. Click Save and then Deploy to make the data access control available for use. 
 Step 3 — Apply the data access control to the target object. Open the view or analytic model to be protected. Select the output node of the view and open the Data Access Control list in its side panel. Add the data access control, and in the Join section, map the columns from the object to the criteria columns defined in the data access control. Deploy the object to activate row-level filtering. 
 A data access control applied to a source view is propagated downstream: when a protected view is used as a source for another object, any data access control applied to that source appears under Applied via Sources in the consuming object. Users of the consuming object will see only the records they are authorised to view based on upstream protection. A single data access control can be applied to multiple views. 
 For data products delivered as intelligent content through SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP explicitly states that all intelligent content is secured in SAP Datasphere through data access controls. However, any authorisations that are applied to data in the source system are not imported automatically when the data is delivered to Datasphere. The Space Administrator must therefore prepare the permissions entity and apply the appropriate data access control to the delivered objects. 
 SAP Cloud Identity Services 
 BDC integrates with the SAP Cloud Identity Services authorisation policy mechanism to extend governance beyond row-level filtering. 
 SAP Cloud Identity Services — Authorization Management provides administrators with a centralised, policy-driven mechanism for governing user access to business applications. Each authorization policy comprises a set of rules that determine which actions a user may perform on specified resources, with conditions driven by user attributes or business object attributes. Policies are authored in Data Control Language (DCL), an SQL-like syntax purpose-built for expressing access control rules precisely and consistently. 
 Conclusion 
 Data product governance in SAP Business Data Cloud is a layered, end-to-end model: domains define ownership; terms and conditions establish usage obligations; the access request lifecycle enforces consent and creates a durable audit trail through access agreements; Data Access Controls in SAP Datasphere ensure that once a data product is installed, each user sees o

title: Setting up OpenCode in Business Application Studio with SAP AI Core
author: felixbartler
text:
Today we are looking at a quick setup of OpenCode in Business Application Studio, using SAP AI Core as the backbone for LLMs. This is useful if you want a coding agent fully enabled by BTP components — without any local installation on your machine. In general this also works in VS Code. 

 Prerequisites 
 Business Application Studio 
 SAP AI Core instance + AI Core service key 
 Resource Group exists in AI Core 
 Orchestration Deployment exists in the Resource Group on AI Core 
 If you are unsure about the AI Core part, check out this tutorial: Provisioning Generative AI Hub in SAP AI Core . 
 Install OpenCode 
 Basically, follow the official installation guide — at the time of writing this is done with the following command: curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash 

 Check if it's working 
 Just type: opencode 
 and see how it loads up. If you are doing this on your local machine, make sure to add it to your shell config ( .bashrc / .zshrc ). 
 Hook up SAP AI Core as integration 
 In OpenCode, use /connect to search for SAP AI Core . Here you need to hand in a service key and submit with Enter. 

 Search for SAP AI Core 

 Paste your AI Core Service Key 

 And select a model. It could be that you are also asked for the thinking effort. Here you will see all the models available in orchestration — see SAP Note 3437766 . 

 Then you can try it out and ask "Hi" — this might work. 
 For me the /connect flow didn't always stick, so the reliable route is to push the service key into the background service directly (use SINGLE quotes — the $ in the clientsecret must stay literal): # 1) Write the service key into the background service as an env var
opencode service set env AICORE_SERVICE_KEY '{"clientid":"<CLIENT_ID>","clientsecret":"<CLIENT_SECRET>","url":"https://<your-tenant>.authentication.sap.hana.ondemand.com","serviceurls":{"AI_API_URL":"https://<ai-api-host>.ml.hana.ondemand.com"}}'

# 2) Set the resource group
opencode service set env AICORE_RESOURCE_GROUP 'default'

# 3) Restart the service so it inherits the env
opencode service restart

# 4) Verify the credential was registered
opencode auth list | grep -i "sap ai core" 
 So: first create the AI Core integration, then restart OpenCode with the new environment. From here the credentials are set — but there is one more thing before the agent actually works. 
 Hitting "Schema validation failed"? 
 The moment you ask for something real — build a plan, create an agent, use a tool — you will likely see the turn fall apart like this, with Error: Schema validation failed after every message: 

 A plain "hi" may still answer (with that error trailing behind it), but anything that makes the agent plan or call a tool dies and nothing renders. Third-party "free" models (DeepSeek and friends) work fine, which makes it look like an AI Core problem — it isn't. 
 TL;DR — you need an OpenCode config. Create opencode.json (global at ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json , or in your project root) with this one override, then opencode service restart : {
 "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
 "provider": {
 "sap-ai-core": {
 "npm": "@jerome-benoit/sap-ai-provider@5.1.2"
 }
 }
} 
 Nothing else changes — same service key, same models, same model IDs. That's the whole fix. It pins the provider SDK to a later version. In future you might need to go even higher than 5.1.2. 
 Why this happens 
 OpenCode (≥ 2.4) talks to providers through the AI SDK V3 interface, where a finish reason is an object { normalized, raw } validated against a fixed set ( stop | length | tool-calls | content-filter | error | unknown ). But the model registry wires sap-ai-core to the provider's V2 package, where the finish reason is a plain string. The V2→V3 bridge turns "unknown" (and anything it can't classify) into "other" — a value OpenCode's own schema rejects, so the turn is dropped. 
 The override above simply points sap-ai-core at the provider's V3 package ( @Jerome -benoit/sap-ai-provider ) instead of the -v2 one, which emits the object shape OpenCode expects. I pinned it to 5.1.2 (the version this post was tested on); drop the @5.1.2 if you'd rather always pull the latest. 
 This is tracked upstream — models.dev#14467 (registry should point at the V3 package) and opencode#66153 (the finish-reason bridge). Once either lands, you can drop the override entirely. Full write-up and a reproducible before/after script: opencode-sap-ai-core-fix . 
 The result 
 With the config in place, restart and the same prompt that blew up before now runs end to end — the agent explores the workspace, reads files, calls tools, and builds its plan, all on GPT-6.1 Sol · SAP AI Core : 

 From here you have a fully working coding agent on SAP AI Core — start it with opencode , pick your model with /models (e.g. sap-ai-core/anthropic--claude-4.6-sonnet , sap-ai-core/gpt-6.1-sol ), and go. 
 Alternative 
 Also check out the setup with Cline as an alternative: Using Cline with SAP AI Core in VS Code — A Complete Setup Guide .

title: From Firefighting to Engineering: Performance, MCP/AI & Migration for SAP Commerce Cloud
author: cuikenjian
text:
Running an SAP Commerce Cloud project means dealing with problems that rarely have clean textbook answers. How do you test performance in a way that actually reflects what happens on launch day? Can AI tooling genuinely save time in day-to-day Commerce Cloud development, or is it still more hype than help? And when the time comes to leave Accelerator behind , how do you avoid rebuilding the same technical debt in a different framework? 
 These are the kinds of questions we hear regularly from project teams — and they are exactly what the next three live sessions, organized in coordination with SAP Expert Services , set out to address. Each session is rooted in patterns and lessons from real customer engagements, with live demos and concrete examples rather than product overviews. 
 Session 1 — Performance Testing Strategy & Production Optimization Best Practices 
 Performance issues in SAP Commerce Cloud tend to surface at the worst possible moment — during peak traffic, during go-live, or in a support ticket from a frustrated end user. By that point, the team is already firefighting. 
 This session walks through how to approach performance testing as a structured, iterative engineering discipline rather than a last-minute checkbox. It covers both the frontend and backend dimensions of the architecture: 
 Frontend (SSR) realities — Why Node.js single-threading and Server-Side Rendering create challenges that don't exist in a traditional browser context, and why local SSR profiling should be your first move. 
 Building a representative test — How to set up a stage environment that mirrors production, define meaningful KPIs, and write JMeter scripts that reflect actual traffic distribution rather than synthetic load. 
 Database optimization — Capacity planning with the Hyperscale model, the effect of large tables on SQL query time, read replica offloading for heavy backend processing, and a data cleanup discipline that prevents silent degradation over time. 
 Blocking calls and thread pool saturation — How synchronous external calls (payment providers, ERPs, third-party services) can exhaust the thread pool, and what to do about it architecturally. 
 CPU profiling and caching — Using Dynatrace thread dumps to find method hotspots, and applying a bottom-up caching strategy: region cache → CMS cache → OCC API cache → CDN. 
 For context on why this matters beyond the technical layer: research cited in the session shows that every 0.1 second improvement in mobile load time correlates with an 8.4% increase in conversion rate and a 9.2% lift in average order value. 
 Relevant for: Commerce architects, platform engineers, technical consultants, project managers, and anyone responsible for storefront reliability under real-world traffic. 
 Session 2 — Boost Your SAP Commerce Cloud Project with MCP Server and AI Assistant 
 A typical Commerce Cloud developer's morning often looks like this: open HAC to run a FlexibleSearch query, switch to Backoffice to inspect a type, jump to Postman to test an OCC endpoint, then wrestle with ImpEx syntax in yet another tool. Each switch breaks focus, and much of this work is repetitive boilerplate. 
 This session introduces mcp-local-ccv2 — a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that connects an AI assistant directly to a running SAP Commerce Cloud instance. The idea is straightforward: tasks like FlexibleSearch queries, ImpEx imports, OCC inspection, and Groovy maintenance scripts become natural-language conversations, executed without leaving the chat window. 
 The session covers: 
 What this tool is and what it is not — A clear distinction between mcp-local-ccv2 (a developer productivity tool from SAP Expert Services for dev/staging environments) and SAP's official Storefront MCP Server (a product-grade tool for storefront interactions). Same protocol, entirely different purpose and audience. 
 Architecture and communication flow — How a natural-language prompt becomes a FlexibleSearch query or ImpEx import, step by step, with all processing running locally on your machine. 
 Four capability areas, demonstrated live — HAC tools (FlexibleSearch, Groovy scripting, cache management), OCC tools (product, catalog, cart, and order inspection), Integration API inspection, and ImpEx generation and execution. 
 Setup walkthrough — Prerequisites (Node.js v18+, a running CCV2 instance, an MCP-compatible AI client such as Joule Work, Claude Desktop, Cursor, or VS Code Copilot), configuration, and security safeguards including scoped HAC users, local-only execution, and confirmation prompts before any write operation. 
 Practical adoption patterns — Using the tool for onboarding new developers, seeding test data on feature branches, building a shared prompt library, and integrating MCP-assisted work into daily standups and code reviews. 
 Field experience suggests that up to 30% of routine development tasks can be automated or executed significantly faster with this approach. 
 Relevant for: Commerce Cloud developers, technical consultants, solution architects, and project leads looking to reduce context-switching in daily development work. 
 Session 3 — Tips and Tricks for Migrating from Accelerator Storefront to Composable Storefront 
 SAP has confirmed that the deprecated Accelerator UI template extensions will not be removed in a future release — there is no hard deadline forcing your hand. But Accelerator is also not receiving new platform capabilities, and the gap widens with every release. AI-based commerce features, Progressive Web App support, cleaner CI/CD separation — all of these require a headless front end. 
 The question most project teams are dealing with is not whether to migrate, but how to do it without rebuilding all the same complexity in Angular . This session shares practical lessons from real migration projects, focused on doing less work for a better result. 
 Three themes run through the session: 
 Classify before you estimate. The most common migration mistake is treating every Accelerator finding as a development task. Instead, the session introduces a five-category classification — Keep Standard, Reconfigure, Rebuild, Extend API, or Retire — that is applied before any estimate is assigned. A concrete example walks through a Product Details Page with five customizations that, after reassessment, reduced to two actual development tasks. The rest were resolved through standard capabilities, CMS configuration, or retirement. 
 Use what Composable Storefront already gives you. Teams consistently underestimate what is already available out of the box. CMS-driven layouts and slot configuration can replace many JSP layout customizations without writing Angular code. The styleClasses attribute on CMS components enables visual variations managed by content editors, not developers. And the OCC API exposes significantly more data than most teams realize — a common mistake is building a new OCC extension for data that is already in the Product, Cart, or BaseSite response. 
 Phase the migration, don't rewrite everything at once. The session outlines a parallel-storefront strategy where Accelerator and Composable Storefront run side by side on the same backend. Pages and journeys are migrated incrementally — search and category pages first, checkout last — allowing the team to validate architecture decisions in production before full commitment. Projects following this approach have reported conversion rate improvements from 2.5% to 3.0%, developer velocity gains of up to 200%, and payback periods as short as six months. 
 Relevant for: Commerce Cloud developers, technical consultants, solution architects, and project leads who are planning or actively executing a migration from Accelerator. 
 Registration 
 All three sessions are live-only — no recordings will be made available. Check the registration pages for upcoming dates:

 Looking forward to seeing you in the live sessions and happy learning!

title: SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model: Default Release Cadence Change
author: MarijaRistinSremcevic
text:
Hello administrators, 
 Starting December 10, 2026, the default release cadence for SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model (SAP PaPM Cloud SM) changes: Fast Track mode is now switched on by default . 
 This means your tenants will automatically receive Standard Model updates on a weekly basis, unless you choose to opt out and switch to the Slow Track cadence which delivers updates once a month. 
 Why This Change? 
 Switching to Fast Track as the default setting is designed to benefit you as an administrator and your end users in several ways: 
 Faster access to fixes and improvements 
 With weekly updates, corrections and enhancements reach your tenants sooner. You no longer have to wait up to a month for a fix to arrive. 
 Smaller, more predictable updates 
 Frequent, incremental deliveries mean each update is smaller in scope, easier to review, and less likely to introduce unexpected behavior compared to large monthly batches. 
 Higher overall stability 
 Issues are identified and resolved earlier in the update cycle, reducing the risk of your tenants running on a version with known defects for an extended period. 
 Continued flexibility 
 Both release cadences remain available. If monthly updates better suit your organization's change management processes, you can switch to Slow Track mode at any time. 
 Background 
 In October 2025, SAP PaPM Cloud SM introduced the option to choose between two release cadences, as described in SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model - Introducing Release Cadence Settings . 
 At the time, the default was a monthly delivery of updates. Administrators who wanted more frequent deliveries could opt in to Fast Track mode, available in Administration > Settings, to receive updates on a weekly basis, with freeze periods at the beginning and end of each month. 
 As of December 10, 2026, this default is reversed: Fast Track mode is now the default setting, and administrators who prefer monthly updates can opt out and switch to a cadence now referred to as Slow Track . 
 How Does This Change Affect My Tenants? 
 With this upgrade, all customers who have not customized the default release cadence settings for their tenants will be automatically switched to Fast Track mode. Those who had changed this setting before will remain on their chosen release cadence. 
 Existing Customers 
 Depending on the previous release cadence settings configuration of your tenants, the following steps should be performed: 

 Current Fast Track mode status 
 Was this setting customized? 
 Status after December 10 
 Action required after December 10 

 Fast Track mode inactive 
 No 

 Fast Track mode active 
 No action required to stay on Fast Track. 
 To switch to Slow Track and receive updates monthly, deactivate Fast Track mode in Settings . 

 Fast Track mode inactive 
 Yes 
 Fast Track mode inactive 
 No action required. Your setting remains unchanged. 

 Fast Track mode active 
 Yes 
 Fast Track mode active 
 No action required. Your setting remains unchanged. 

 New Customers 

 Fast Track mode status in Settings 
 Action required 

 Fast Track mode active ( default ) 
 No action required to stay on Fast Track. 
 To switch to monthly updates, deactivate Fast Track mode in Administration > Settings . 

 How to Switch to Slow Track 
 If your organization prefers monthly updates, you can deactivate Fast Track mode at any time: 
 Go to Home > Administration > Settings . 
 Under Release Cadence Settings , deactivate the Fast Track mode toggle. 
 Note: Deactivating Fast Track mode does not take effect immediately. The switch to monthly updates takes effect with the next scheduled monthly release. If you reactivate Fast Track mode, the change takes effect immediately. 
 Remember: Environments exported from a Fast Track system can be imported into a system running on any release cadence. If the destination system is on the monthly release cadence (Slow Track), you can either switch the destination to Fast Track mode first, or wait for the next monthly release before importing. 

 Questions? 
 If you have questions about the release cadence options or need guidance on which cadence is right for your organization, post a comment here or reach out to us through SAP support.

title: The Importance of GSI Scope Identification in an SAP S/4HANA Implementation
author: atshayarr
text:
SAP S/4HANA Implementation: Why Getting the GSI Scope Right Matters More Than We Think 
 Lessons and observations from participating in SAP S/4HANA implementation and scope identification discussions 
 Introduction 
 One of the interesting things about being involved in SAP S/4HANA implementation discussions is realizing that the actual implementation journey begins much earlier than configuration. 
 Before discussing configuration, developments, integrations, or testing, there is one important question that needs to be answered: 
 Are we implementing the right business processes in the first place? 
 This is where Global Scope Item (GSI) identification and scope validation become important. 
 Having participated in SAP S/4HANA implementation and GSI scope identification discussions, I have come to appreciate that identifying the scope is not simply about reviewing an Excel sheet and marking items as Yes or No. It involves understanding business requirements, evaluating process applicability, identifying dependencies, and ensuring that the proposed SAP solution aligns with the organization's actual business needs. 
 Sometimes, a functionality may look relevant at a high level, but when we start reviewing the detailed process variants, we may realize that not all of them are required. 
 This is one of the reasons I believe scope identification deserves much more attention during an SAP implementation. 
 In this article, I would like to share some practical observations about GSI scope identification, particularly from an SAP S/4HANA Finance and Controlling (FICO) perspective. 
 1. Understanding GSI Scope Identification 
 For anyone who is relatively new to SAP implementation projects, let's first understand what GSI scope identification means. 
 Global Scope Items represent predefined business processes and capabilities available for an SAP solution. During an SAP S/4HANA implementation, organizations evaluate the relevant scope items to determine which business processes are required for their operations. 
 The objective is not to implement every available SAP functionality. 
 Instead, the objective is to identify the processes that are relevant to the organization's business model, operational requirements, reporting needs, and future objectives. 
 For example, during an SAP FICO scope assessment, the discussion may cover: 
 Financial Accounting (FI) 

 General Ledger Accounting 

 Accounts Payable 

 Accounts Receivable 

 Asset Accounting 

 Bank Accounting 

 Financial Closing 
 Controlling (CO) 

 Cost Center Accounting 

 Profit Center Accounting 

 Internal Orders 

 Product Costing 

 Overhead Cost Accounting 

 Universal Allocation 

 Margin Analysis 

 Material Ledger and Actual Costing 
 However, identifying these processes at a high level is only the beginning. The actual challenge is understanding which detailed functionalities and process variants are applicable. 
 2. A GSI Marked as "Yes" Does Not Mean Every Process Variant Is Required 
 This is one of the important aspects I would like to highlight. 
 During scope identification, teams sometimes focus heavily on the high-level scope item without spending sufficient time reviewing its detailed process variants. 
 Let's consider a practical example from SAP Controlling. 
 Suppose an organization confirms that Cost Center Accounting is required. 
 Does that automatically mean every available Cost Center Accounting-related functionality should also be included? 
 Not necessarily. 
 The organization may require cost center planning, actual cost monitoring, and reporting. However, certain allocation methods or other process variants may not be relevant to its current business requirements. 
 This is why reviewing the detailed scope hierarchy is important. 
 Depending on the scope structure being used, the review may extend across: 

 Level 1 – High-level business process. 

 Level 2 – Process category. 

 Level 3 – Sub-process. 

 Level 4 – Detailed process variant. 
 The exact hierarchy may vary depending on the scope documentation. 
 My observation: Scope validation should not stop at identifying whether a GSI is applicable. We should also understand which individual process variants are actually required. 
 This small distinction can make a significant difference during solution design and implementation. 
 3. Why a Simple Yes/No Decision Requires Proper Business Understanding 
 One common approach during GSI scope assessment is to maintain a Yes/No applicability status against each scope item. 
 Although this looks straightforward, arriving at the correct decision requires proper discussion. 
 I would suggest considering three possible statuses: 
 YES – Applicable 
 The business process is required and should be considered within the implementation scope. 
 NO – Not Applicable 
 The process is not required based on the organization's business requirements and the agreed implementation scope. 
 PENDING – Further Discussion Required 
 The applicability is not yet confirmed and requires additional clarification, internal discussion, or stakeholder approval. 
 I particularly believe that the third category is important. 
 In practical scope discussions, there may be items for which the business team does not immediately have a clear answer. 
 Instead of making assumptions and marking them as No, it is better to keep them open until the relevant stakeholders arrive at a decision. 
 For example, consider certain Costing-related line items associated with Statistical Key Figures. 
 Before deciding whether these are applicable, it is important to understand how the organization uses statistical figures, whether they support any allocation processes, and whether there are related reporting requirements. 
 A decision should be based on the actual business requirement rather than an assumption. 
 An item left blank is not necessarily an item that is not required. It may simply be an item that needs further discussion. 
 4. The Importance of Understanding Cross-Module Dependencies 
 Another important aspect of scope identification is understanding that SAP modules do not operate independently. 
 A decision taken by one functional team can have implications for another module. 
 Let's take a simple procurement example. 
 When a company procures materials, the process may involve: 

 Purchase Requisition. 

 Purchase Order. 

 Goods Receipt. 

 Invoice Receipt. 

 Vendor Payment. 
 Although this appears to be primarily an MM process, it has important implications for Finance. 
 Goods movements may trigger accounting entries, invoice postings affect Accounts Payable, and subsequent payments impact bank and general ledger accounts. 
 Similarly, in a manufacturing environment, production activities can influence inventory valuation, Product Costing, and Financial Accounting. 
 This is why I believe GSI scope identification should involve cross-functional discussions rather than being handled independently by individual module teams. 
 A scope item that appears unnecessary from one functional perspective may have dependencies that need to be evaluated by another team. 
 5. Common Challenges During GSI Scope Identification 
 Based on the nature of SAP implementation and scope identification discussions, there are several areas that deserve particular attention. 
 1. Incomplete understanding of business requirements 
 Sometimes, business teams are not entirely clear about their future requirements during the initial discussions. Additional clarification may be necessary before finalizing the scope. 
 2. Marking items without understanding their purpose 
 Selecting Yes or No simply based on a scope description can lead to incorrect decisions. The business purpose of the functionality should be understood first. 
 3. Overlooking detailed process variants 
 Confirming a high-level GSI without reviewing the associated lower-level processes can result in an incomplete scope assessment. 
 4. Lack of clarity on responsibilities 
 When business owners, functional consultants, and demonstrators are not clearly identified, follow-up discussions and confirmations can become difficult. 
 5. Delayed decisions on open items 
 Pending scope items should be tracked properly. Otherwise, unresolved decisions may affect subsequent design and implementation activities. 
 6. Changes after scope sign-off 
 New requirements may emerge after scope confirmation. These should be evaluated through an appropriate change-control process rather than being added without assessing their impact. 
 6. My Recommended Approach for Effective GSI Scope Validation 
 Based on my participation in implementation and scope identification discussions, I believe a structured approach makes the exercise more effective. 
 Here are some practices I would recommend. 
 Step 1: Understand the Business Process First 
 Before reviewing individual scope items, understand how the business currently operates and what it expects from the future SAP solution. 
 Step 2: Review the Detailed Scope 
 Do not limit the assessment to GSI IDs and descriptions. Review the detailed process variants and understand their business relevance. 
 Step 3: Maintain a Structured Scope Tracker 
 An Excel-based tracker can be very useful for managing the assessment. 
 I would recommend including the following information: 

 GSI ID and description. 

 Module and sub-module. 

 Detailed process variants. 

 Applicability status (Yes/No/Pending). 

 Responsible business owner. 

 Responsible functional consultant. 

 Primary and backup FTS demonstrator, where applicable. 

 Remarks and clarification requirements. 

 Final confirmation or sign-off status. 
 Step 4: Maintain a Separate List of Open Items 
 Not every decision can be finalized in the first discussion. 
 Maintain a separate list of pending items, assign responsibilities, and follow up with the concerned stakeholders. 
 Step 5: Discuss Cross-Functional Dependencies 
 Involve the relevant FI, CO, MM, SD, PP, and other functional teams wherever integration dependencies exist. 
 Step 6: Document the Reason Behind Important Decisions 
 A Yes or No status alone may not explain why a particular process was included or excluded. 
 Documenting the reasoning helps avoid repeated discussions and provides clarity during future project phases. 
 Step 7: Obtain the Necessary Sign-Off 
 Once the scope assessment is completed, ensure that the relevant business stakeholders review and confirm the final scope. 
 Any subsequent changes should be managed through the agreed project governance process. 
 7. What Can Happen When Scope Is Not Properly Validated? 
 This is where the importance of the entire exercise becomes more evident. 
 Imagine a situation where a business process is incorrectly marked as not applicable during the initial scope review. 
 Later, during solution design or testing, the business team identifies that the functionality is actually required. 
 At that point, the project team may need to revisit the scope, evaluate the solution design, perform additional configuration, update documentation, and conduct further testing. 
 Similarly, including unnecessary functionalities can increase implementation effort without delivering corresponding business value. 
 Some possible consequences include: 

 Rework during solution design. 

 Additional configuration and development efforts. 

 Unexpected integration dependencies. 

 Increased testing effort. 

 Delays in business sign-off. 

 Additional project costs. 

 Scope changes during later implementation stages. 
 This is why I believe it is always better to spend sufficient time understanding and validating the scope at the beginning rather than resolving avoidable gaps during later project phases. 
 8. A Few Questions Every SAP Consultant Should Ask During Scope Identification 
 I personally feel that asking the right questions is just as important as reviewing the scope documentation. 
 Whenever
